title: AI Is Forcing Data Centers To Rethink Trust
gist: AI-driven data center scaling is forcing a shift from perimeter-based security controls to zero-trust, evidence-backed 'trust' architectures spanning the entire hardware supply chain, with physically unclonable functions, hardware roots of trust (Caliptra), and post-quantum cryptography readiness emerging as critical but increasingly costly and certification-bottlenecked requirements.

themes.theme: Shift from security controls to zero-trust, evidence-based trust

insights.claim: A Middle East customer scrapped an entire order of servers after a 48-hour gap in shipment logistics tracking meant no one could attest to the security of the boxes, illustrating that even brief provenance gaps can trigger total write-offs of hardware in security-conscious deployments.
insights.speaker: Scott Register (Keysight Technologies)
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that supply-chain provenance gaps have real, immediate financial cost (full order write-offs) — validates strong demand for continuous chain-of-custody/attestation technology and is a cautionary data point for hardware logistics providers serving security-sensitive buyers.
insights.quote: One of our customers in the Middle East trashed a huge order of servers because they traced the logistics of the shipment, and there was one period of 48 hours where no one could attest to the security of all those boxes. So they scrapped them.
insights.locator: Register anecdote, path to zero trust section

insights.claim: The industry's security paradigm is shifting from 'controls' (antivirus, firewalls) to 'trust' — defined as confidence backed by evidence — starting with the supply chain as the foundational domain of trust.
insights.speaker: Scott Register (Keysight Technologies)
insights.so_what: A useful mental model (controls vs. evidence-backed trust) for evaluating which security vendors are ahead of the curve — those building attestation/evidence infrastructure vs. those still selling traditional perimeter controls.
insights.quote: Historically, we thought about controls, antivirus, or firewalls. Now we're moving from thinking about controls to thinking about trust. If security is having the controls in place, then trust is having confidence backed by evidence.
insights.locator: Register quote, path to zero trust section

insights.claim: Remote physical attacks against data centers can only be mitigated by a paradigm shift toward dynamic security boundaries — locking digitally signed, verified identities to software images and dynamic virtual machines — as conventional static domain-isolation approaches reach their limits and company networks evolve toward zero-trust architectures away from traditional firewalls.
insights.speaker: Peter Laackmann (Infineon Technologies)
insights.so_what: Infineon is positioning hardware-anchored dynamic identity (secure elements + signed VM images) as the successor architecture to firewalls — a specific technology bet data center security buyers and competing vendors should track.
insights.quote: Conventional approaches for security domain isolation reach their limits and will be widely replaced by dynamic boundaries — for example, by locking digitally signed and verified identities to software images and dynamic virtual machines.

insights.claim: Certified secure elements combined with security-hardened MCUs form an 'ideal symbiosis' enabling the three pillars of information security — confidentiality, integrity, and availability — that data centers require under a zero-trust model.
insights.speaker: Peter Laackmann (Infineon Technologies)
insights.so_what: Reinforces secure-element + hardened-MCU as the specific hardware product pairing Infineon is selling into data center zero-trust builds — a concrete BOM-level opportunity.
insights.quote: State-of-the-art security components like certified secure elements and security-hardened MCUs build an ideal symbiosis to enable the three elements of information security crucial for data centers — confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

themes.theme: Physically unclonable functions (PUFs) as supply-chain traceability anchor

insights.claim: Physically unclonable functions (PUFs), after nearly two decades of slow growth, have emerged as a cornerstone technology for supply chain tracking — acting as an unforgeable 'passport' anchor for identity and traceability as hardware moves through manufacturing, testing, assembly and deployment.
insights.speaker: Sylvain Guilley (Secure-IC, a Cadence company)
insights.so_what: After ~20 years of slow adoption, PUF technology is reaching an inflection point of real commercial deployment driven by AI-era supply-chain trust needs — a technology-maturity signal for investors tracking hardware security IP vendors like Secure-IC/Cadence.
insights.quote: Following nearly two decades of slow growth, physically unclonable functions (PUFs) have emerged as a cornerstone technology for supply chain tracking.

insights.claim: PUF-based chain-of-custody technology lets an organization trace the full history and identity of a hardware component and every action performed on it (hardware and software) until deployment, addressing the risk of gaps or attackers infiltrating an ecosystem between manufacturing stages.
insights.speaker: Sylvain Guilley (Secure-IC, a Cadence company)
insights.so_what: Chain-of-custody/provenance tracking is becoming a standard requirement, not an add-on, for hyperscale data center hardware — a durable licensing/IP revenue stream for security IP vendors.
insights.quote: You can trace the provenance and identity, and all the actions performed on the hardware and software system, until you reach the final state where you can deploy and kickstart your data center.

insights.claim: Runtime firmware/infrastructure integrity monitoring (measured boot, real-time integrity monitoring) is currently one of the least-monitored areas for attacks in data centers, despite hardware silicon security's growing importance and the requirement that device identity be anti-tamper and impossible to compromise or clone.
insights.speaker: Dana Neustadter (Synopsys)
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, underserved gap (runtime firmware integrity monitoring) as the next likely area of security product investment and M&A in data center hardware security.
insights.quote: Then you have firmware and infrastructure. You want to scan for vulnerabilities. Typically, here you use measured boot or real-time integrity monitoring. Today this is one of the areas that is the least monitored for attacks during runtime.

themes.theme: Defense-in-depth is evolving from more layers to smarter layers

insights.claim: Historically, security-in-depth was treated as a 'best practice' rather than a hard requirement at the silicon level, meaning vendors could skip it to save die area or engineering time; this is no longer acceptable as multi-layered defense becomes mandatory rather than optional.
insights.speaker: Reed Hinkel (Synopsys)
insights.so_what: Security features are moving from optional/best-practice to mandatory silicon requirements, meaning die area and engineering budget increasingly must be allocated to security by default — a structural cost increase (and revenue opportunity for security IP) across the chip industry.
insights.quote: From a silicon perspective, it was always treated as a best practice, but what does that mean? If it's a best practice, that means it's not a requirement; therefore, I don't have to include it.
insights.locator: Hinkel quote on best practice vs requirement

insights.claim: Every component and sub-component in a data center — confidential compute, hardware silicon security, firmware/infrastructure, network security, access management, virtualization, AI model protection, and training infrastructure protection — must be individually trusted, with every connection and dialog between them authenticated and proven, representing a fundamental shift in data center security scope.
insights.speaker: Dana Neustadter (Synopsys)
insights.so_what: Defines the full addressable surface for data center security spend — investors can map named categories (confidential compute, AI model protection, training infrastructure protection) directly to specific vendor product lines to assess exposure.
insights.quote: You need to have this trust around every single component and components within components... Everything needs to be protected, and whatever connection and dialog those components have needs to be authenticated and proven.

insights.claim: Defense-in-depth is shifting from simply adding more protective layers toward making existing layers intelligent, adaptive, and continuously verifiable under zero-trust and assume-breach principles, where the goal is not just to prevent attacks but to limit impact once a breach occurs, requiring hardware roots of trust, cryptographic agility, and secure update mechanisms that can respond to new threats without full redesign.
insights.speaker: Ajay Kapoor (Rambus)
insights.so_what: Explicit framework shift (more layers -> smarter layers, assume-breach) that should reshape how investors evaluate security product roadmaps — value increasingly lies in adaptive/updatable hardware roots of trust rather than static protection stacking.
insights.quote: Today, the emphasis is shifting toward making those layers intelligent, adaptive, and continuously verifiable... the goal is not only to prevent attacks, but also to limit their impact when they occur.

themes.theme: Cost and complexity of expanding trust boundaries

insights.claim: Expanding data center trust boundaries and hardware footprint incurs multiple compounding costs: larger silicon footprint for cryptography (now needing post-quantum crypto and crypto-agility across multiple algorithms/key sizes/modes), formal certification (versus casual auditing previously), verification cost, deployment cost, and ongoing configuration/verification cost.
insights.speaker: Sylvain Guilley (Secure-IC, a Cadence company)
insights.so_what: Quantifies a real, multi-dimensional cost increase (silicon area, certification, verification, deployment) tied directly to PQC/crypto-agility adoption — a structural margin headwind for chipmakers but a revenue tailwind for security-IP and certification service providers.
insights.quote: Now, cryptography is getting fat. We have post-quantum cryptography, and crypto-agility to support multiple algorithms, key sizes, and modes of operation... now it must be certified. This incurs a cost in verification, but also a cost in silicon.
insights.locator: Guilley quote on costs of trust

insights.claim: Securing data center AI models specifically requires four essential components: defending data input from poisoning, protecting the model from tampering, defending against manipulation of the data processing step, and verifying the AI output — often requiring multiple layers of digital signing (model signed by a secure element; output data digitally signed to indicate provenance).
insights.speaker: Peter Laackmann (Infineon Technologies)
insights.so_what: A concrete four-part checklist for AI model security investors can use to evaluate whether a given vendor's product actually covers the full AI-model trust chain versus addressing only one link.
insights.quote: Defending the data input from poisoning; Protecting the model from tampering; Defending against manipulation of the data processing step; and Verifying the AI output.
insights.locator: Laackmann's list of AI model security components

themes.theme: Caliptra, chiplets, and PQC deadlines reshape standards

insights.claim: Open-source hardware root-of-trust projects like Caliptra (Open Compute Project Foundation) are becoming essential as chiplet-based composable hardware — where different pieces of a chip package come from different manufacturers — requires establishing lower-level trust between chiplets that must communicate, moving beyond old-school monolithic system-on-chip trust models.
insights.speaker: Scott Register (Keysight Technologies)
insights.so_what: Chiplet disaggregation (multiple vendors' silicon in one package) creates a new inter-chiplet trust requirement that open standards like Caliptra are positioned to solve — relevant for anyone tracking chiplet ecosystem standardization and OCP-aligned vendors.
insights.quote: I'm now using composable hardware with chiplets that need to talk to each other. Little pieces of those different chiplets may come from different manufacturers, but they must trust each other.
insights.locator: Register quote on Caliptra and chiplets

insights.claim: Caliptra's adoption is driven partly by NIST standards data centers must comply with to operate as government cloud workload carriers, and partly by a U.S. executive order timeline requiring anything running GovCloud workloads to be post-quantum secure beginning next year (2027).
insights.speaker: Reed Hinkel (Synopsys)
insights.so_what: A hard regulatory deadline (PQC required for GovCloud workloads starting 2027) creates a concrete, dated catalyst for PQC hardware/IP adoption — investors should track vendor readiness against this specific timeline.
insights.quote: Data centers are on an accelerated path where anything that runs GovCloud, beginning next year, has to be post-quantum secure.

insights.claim: Because systems deployed today may still need to protect sensitive information a decade or more into the future, cryptographic agility (architectures that can accommodate future crypto transitions rather than hard-coding specific algorithms) is becoming a critical design objective, shifting the industry focus from selecting algorithms to ensuring infrastructure can evolve as standards and threats change.
insights.speaker: Ajay Kapoor (Rambus)
insights.so_what: Crypto-agility (not a specific PQC algorithm) is the durable investable feature — favors IP vendors building updatable/agile security architectures over those hard-coding a single current-generation algorithm.
insights.quote: Data center operators recognize that systems deployed today may still be responsible for protecting sensitive information a decade or more into the future, making cryptographic agility a critical design objective.

insights.claim: A growing backlog in FIPS 140-3 product certifications is creating its own supply chain bottleneck: many vendors delayed certification and now face a huge backlog that is expected to worsen, risking products sitting unsold on shelves because government buyers cannot purchase uncertified products.
insights.speaker: Reed Hinkel (Synopsys)
insights.so_what: A specific, named regulatory bottleneck (FIPS 140-3 certification backlog) could delay revenue recognition for PQC-hardware vendors selling into government/GovCloud markets — a concrete near-term risk factor to monitor in vendor guidance and order backlogs.
insights.quote: The big challenge is that they're already running a huge backlog. It's only going to get worse because everyone's put off getting things certified... It's going to be sitting on a shelf because the government can't buy it.

themes.theme: Convergence of physical and cyber attack surfaces

insights.claim: National-level critical infrastructure (AI data centers, emergency management, healthcare systems) runs on fairly brittle Critical National Infrastructure systems, and there is a fundamental lack of understanding of how interdependent everything has become — a risk the author argues is not being taken seriously enough at either the individual data center or national level.
insights.speaker: Scott Register (Keysight Technologies)
insights.so_what: A strong, explicitly stated warning that national critical infrastructure interdependency is under-appreciated as a systemic risk — relevant for infrastructure resilience investment and policy-risk assessment around AI data center buildouts.
insights.quote: If you just think of it on the national level, we are not taking the threat of cyber-physical seriously enough... They are on fairly brittle Critical National Infrastructure systems.
insights.locator: Register quote on national infrastructure risk

insights.claim: Operators are increasingly concerned with multi-stage attack chains exploiting weaknesses across physical, cyber, and operational domains simultaneously — including physical tampering, supply chain compromise, credential theft, firmware attacks, ransomware, and large-scale DDoS — rather than isolated single-vector attacks, because such chains target foundational trust boundaries and are harder to detect early.
insights.speaker: Ajay Kapoor (Rambus)
insights.so_what: Reinforces that point-solution security products are insufficient; integrated cross-domain (physical + cyber + OT) detection platforms are the direction of demand — favors vendors offering unified rather than siloed security stacks.
insights.quote: Threats such as physical tampering, supply chain compromise, credential theft, firmware attacks, ransomware, and large-scale DDoS campaigns remain particularly concerning because they target foundational trust boundaries and can be difficult to detect early.

insights.claim: Timing-based attacks are an underappreciated threat to power grids and data centers: as SDRs and drones get cheaper, large-scale jamming or spoofing of satellite timing signals becomes more feasible, and even millisecond-level clock desynchronization (not seconds or minutes) can cause serious problems for synchronized grid infrastructure — a resiliency gap the author says gets nowhere near enough attention.
insights.speaker: Scott Register (Keysight Technologies)
insights.so_what: A specific, highly technical and underpriced risk (GPS/timing spoofing against grid-synchronized infrastructure) that could become a tail-risk catalyst for grid/data-center outages — worth flagging for infrastructure risk models and potentially an emerging niche market (anti-spoofing timing hardware).
insights.quote: As SDRs, radios, get cheaper and drones get cheaper, it becomes much more feasible to think about large-scale attacks that either jam or spoof satellite signals... I'm talking milliseconds off, and these bad things will happen.

insights.claim: Sensors and cameras equipped with secure elements can provide trusted authentication of devices and their data, while security-hardened MCUs enable secure processing, encryption, storage and distribution of sensitive data, substantially reducing the effort needed to merge physical and digital security systems as remote physical attacks rise.
insights.speaker: Peter Laackmann (Infineon Technologies)
insights.so_what: Concrete product answer (secure-element-equipped sensors/cameras + hardened MCUs) to the physical-cyber convergence problem — another specific Infineon product angle in the data-center-security supply chain.
insights.quote: Sensors and cameras can be equipped with secure elements that provide trusted authentication of the devices and the data they provide. Security-hardened MCUs allow secure processing, encryption, storage, and distribution of sensitive data.
